title: Rereading chapters 25–26
hookLine: reread the mendicant and the brahmana
carry: the same book, a new reader
tomorrow: what's left of a well-known chant when nobody explains it?

cards: Some last names open doors before the person even says hello. Some school names on an application do the same.
Underneath is a very old question: what makes someone worthy, the family they were born into, or the life they live? The Dhammapada ends on that question.
Its last chapter takes a title people held by birth, brahmana, the priestly class, and asks who really deserves it.

teach.h: NOT BY HAIR, FAMILY OR BIRTH.
teach.b: The answer, in Max Müller's translation: “A man does not become a Brahmana by his platted hair, by his family, or by birth; in whom there is truth and righteousness, he is blessed, he is a Brahmana.”
Then the chapter keeps the title and fills it with a life, verse after verse: him I call a brahmana who is patient, who doesn't cling, who harms no one.

teach.h: A BHIKKHU GUARDS, NOT JUST WEARS.
teach.b: The chapter before it does the same with the word for a monk: a bhikkhu is one who guards eye and ear and tongue, not one who wears the robe. Worth is lived, not inherited.
A neighbor tradition says something close to this in its own words.

teach.h: SAMUEL: THE LORD LOOKS ON THE HEART.
teach.b: In the Hebrew Bible, which Jews and Christians both read, the prophet Samuel goes to choose a king among Jesse's sons, and the tall eldest looks the part. God tells him no.
In the King James Version: “for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart.”
Shared: both refuse to judge by what shows on the outside, the hair, the height, the family. And one honest difference. In Samuel, God is the one who sees the heart and chooses.
In the Dhammapada, no one chooses; the life itself shows who is a brahmana. Same refusal to sort people by birth, two different ways of seeing. That's the reread's last gift.
The first time, this chapter can feel like a long list. Now it reads like the book's closing argument.

teach.h: THE SAME BOOK, A NEW READER.
teach.b: The same book, a new reader.

how: Theravada teachers often point to the Dhammapada's brahmana chapter when they explain that, in the Buddha's teaching, a person's worth comes from conduct rather than birth.

o: a second pass through the monk and the brahmana chapters
a first look at the chapters on fools and on thousands
a list of the rules brahmin priests had to keep

games.q: two texts, one refusal — tap the pairs.
p: how the Dhammapada says no one is a brahmana
the LORD looketh on the heart

s: the Dhammapada's last chapter says brahmins are made by birth
verse 393: not by platted hair, family or birth; truth and righteousness make a brahmana.
in 1 Samuel, the LORD tells Samuel he looks on the heart
1 Samuel 16:7, as Samuel looks over Jesse's sons.
the Dhammapada and 1 Samuel say exactly the same thing
both look past outward things. in Samuel, God sees the heart and chooses; in the Dhammapada, the life itself shows it.

games.q: a new student joins your class from a family nobody's heard of, and someone says she won't fit in here. by the brahmana chapter, what counts?
o: how she lives: truth and kindness, not her family or birth.
her family after all; the verse says lineage settles it.
her grades; the verse says learning is the true mark.
games.why: verse 393 names the outward marks, hair, family, birth, and sets them all aside. what counts is truth and righteousness.

practice: On paper, write one verse you marked this week that you'd have skimmed past the first time. If you kept the ten verses you chose back in year one, write one of those beside it.
Look at the two side by side until the bell, and notice who chose each.

wordCard.voice: Rereading chapters 25 and 26: the mendicant and the brahmana, the Dhammapada's last two chapters. Both take a title and fill it with a way of living.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit: brahmin, the priestly class; the Dhammapada's last chapter, the Brāhmaṇavagga, refills the word.

carryVoice: Keep this one: the same book, a new reader, and worth that's lived, not born. Seven of seven: the Dhammapada, reread.
